An asymptomatic 3-year-old male presents for a routine check-up. On examination you
notice a systolic heart murmur. It is heard best in the lower precordium and has a low, short
tone similar to a plucked string or kazoo. It does not radiate to the axillae or the back and
seems to decrease with inspiration. The remainder of the examination is normal. Which one
of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale:
There are several benign murmurs of childhood that have no association with physiologic or
anatomic abnormalities. Of these, Still’s murmur best fits the murmur described. The cause
of Still’s murmur is unknown, but it may be due to vibrations in the chordae tendinae,
semilunar valves, or ventricular wall. A venous hum consists of a continuous low-pitched
murmur caused by collapse of the jugular veins and their subsequent fluttering, and it
worsens with inspiration or diastole. The murmur of physiologic peripheral pulmonic
stenosis (PPPS) is caused by physiologic changes in the newborn’s pulmonary vessels.
PPPS is a systolic murmur heard loudest in the axillae bilaterally that usually disappears by
9 months of age. Mitral stenosis causes a diastolic murmur, and Eisenmenger’s syndrome involves multiple abnormalities of the heart that cause significant signs and symptoms,
including shortness of breath, cyanosis, and organomegaly, which should become apparent
from a routine history and examination.

text:
A 3-year-old female is brought to your office for a health maintenance examination, and her
father expresses concern about her vision. Her visual acuity is 20/20 bilaterally on a
“tumbling E” visual acuity chart. With both eyes uncovered during a cover/uncover test, the
corneal light reflex in the right eye is medial to the pupil when focused on a fixed point, but
the light reflex in the left eye is almost centered in the pupil. When the left eye is covered,
the right eye moves quickly inward to focus on the fixed point, and the corneal light reflex is
centered in the pupil. When the left eye is uncovered, the right eye returns to its original
position. When you cover the right eye, no left eye movement is noted. Which one of the
following is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale:
Strabismus is an ocular misalignment that can be diagnosed on a cover/uncover test when
the corneal light reflex is deviated from its normal position slightly nasal to mid-pupil. The
misaligned eye then moves to fixate on a held object when the opposite eye is covered. The
eye drifts back to its original position when the opposite eye is uncovered.
Amblyopia is a visual impairment from abnormal visual development - most often as a
result of strabismus. Cataract is a less frequent cause of amblyopia. Esotropia is a type of
strabismus with an inward or nasal deviation of the eye that would be evidenced by a
corneal light reflex lateral to its normal position. (The outward eye deviation seen in this
patient is exotropia.) Heterophoria, or latent strabismus, does not cause eye deviation when
both eyes are uncovered.

text:
Which approach is most appropriate when examining the abdomen and genitals of a ticklish
child?
options: Divert the child’s attention to a picture in the examining room
Place the child’s hands on top of yours for the duration of the examination
Apply increased pressure to the abdomen until the ticklish sensation abates
Ask the child’s parent to hold the child still for the duration of the examination
Ask your office assistant to hold the child still for the duration of the examination
rationale:
A helpful technique when examining any young child is to place the child’s hand on top of
the physician’s hand during the abdominal exam (choice B). This can help divert the child’s
attention if she is ticklish and give the child a sense of control.→ Diversion attempts (choice A) are often unsuccessful with a ticklish child.
→ Applying increased pressure (choice C) may only make the exam more painful to the
patient and thus more difficult.
→ Restraining the child by anyone (choice D and choice E)) will make the exam much
more difficult and potentially more traumatic to the child.

text:
A 17-year-old soccer player presents for a preparticipation examination. His family history
is significant for the autopsy-negative sudden death of his 12-year-old sister while playing
basketball, and for his mother and maternal grandmother having recurrent syncopal
episodes. His medical history and examination are completely normal. Prior to approving
his participation in sports, which one of the following is recommended?
rationale:
A family history of sudden death and recurrent syncope is highly suspicious for genetic
long-QT syndrome. It is best diagnosed with a resting EKG that shows a QTc >460 msec in
females and >440 msec in males. This syndrome especially places young people at risk for
sudden death. Management may include beta-blockers, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, and no participation in competitive sports.
Ref: Roden DM: Long-QT syndrome. N Engl J Med 2008;358(2):169-176.

text:
The parents of a 7-year-old male ask you to evaluate him because of increasing concerns
about his temper tantrums over the past 9 months. He often becomes angry and hostile,
argues with them constantly, and refuses to follow rules or directions. A major source of
difficulty is his refusal to quit playing with his toys when he is asked to come to the dinner
table. After the child ignored repeated attempts to get him to come to the table a few nights
ago, the father became frustrated and told him he had lost his television privileges. In
response, the child became aggressive and destructive, breaking his toys and sweeping his
dinner plate and glass of milk onto the floor. The parents describe many similar scenarios at
bedtime, bath time, and when he is getting dressed. They believe that their son is
deliberately behaving this way to annoy them.
This history is most consistent with:
rationale:
This child meets the DSM-V criteria for oppositional defiant disorder, defined as a pattern of
negativistic, hostile, and defiant behavior lasting at least 6 months. The child will often lose
his or her temper, argue with adults, actively defy or refuse to comply with adults’ requests
or rules, deliberately annoy people, blame others for his or her mistakes or misbehavior, be
easily annoyed by others, appear angry and resentful, or be spiteful or vindictive. At least
four of these behaviors must be present to meet the criteria for diagnosis. The disturbance in
behavior must also cause clinically significant impairment in social, academic, or
occupational functioning, and the behaviors must not occur exclusively during the course of
a psychotic or mood disorder. Meeting the criteria for conduct disorder excludes the
diagnosis of oppositional defiant disorder. If the individual is 18 years of age or older and
meets the criteria for antisocial personality disorder, then oppositional defiant disorder is
excluded.
Oppositional Defiant Disorder

text:
A 15-year-old white female who has had regular periods since age 12 comes to your office
because of secondary amenorrhea and a milky discharge from her breasts. A pregnancy test
is negative.
The best test for initial evaluation of the pituitary in this patient is:
rationale:
Anterior pituitary hormone overproduction is suspected on clinical grounds and confirmed
by appropriate laboratory evaluation. The most common secretory pituitary adenomas are
prolactinomas. They cause galactorrhea and hypogonadism, including amenorrhea,
infertility, and impotence. Growth hormone-secreting tumors, which are the next most
common secretory pituitary tumors, cause acromegaly or gigantism. Next in frequency are
corticotropic (ACTH-secreting) adenomas, which cause cortisol excess (Cushing’s disease).
Glycoprotein hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas (secreting TSH, LH, or FSH) are the
least common. TSH-secreting adenomas are a rare cause of hyperthyroidism. Paradoxically,
most patients with gonadotropin-secreting adenomas have hypogonadism.

text:
An 8-year-old male is brought to your department by his mother, because of bed wetting for
the last 3 weeks. The mother reports that this occurs at night only and it seems to have been
embarrassing for him. She states that it happens about five times a week and has continued
even when the boy was put on fluid restriction after 6 pm for the last 10 days. He has not
lost weight during this period and denies having excessive thirst. The boy had stopped
bedwetting at the age 4 and since then he had never had a similar problem. The mother
denies any changes in the family or stressful events and says that the boy’s nutrition is
regular and he was not on any special diet. Which of the following is the initial step in
management of this patient?
rationale:
This child presents with nocturnal enuresis at the age of 8 after having achieved control over
micturition for 4 years. His condition is considered secondary enuresis, as this is defined as
enuresis occurring 6 months after a child had been continent for at least 6 months. Normally
98% of children achieve daytime continence by the age of 3 while 80% achieve nocturnal
continence by this age. By approximately age 4 years, all children with normal bladder
function should have acquired this ability.When evaluating a child most likely to have secondary enuresis physicians should be alert
for symptoms associated with diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, cystitis, overactive
bladder or dysfunctional voiding, sleep disordered breathing, constipation, urethral
obstruction, and major motor seizure. Psychological problems are also possible causes of
secondary enuresis. The best initial study for screening this patient is urinalysis (choice A).
Cystitis would present with white blood cells and bacteria on urinalysis, while urethral
obstruction may be associated with red blood cells. The presence of glucose would suggest
diabetes mellitus, while a specific gravity greater than 1.020 would rule out diabetes
insipidus.
→ Observation for 2 weeks (choice B) is incorrect. This child has been observed for the last
3 weeks and the best next step is to explore possible causes of enuresis.
→ Desmopressin (choice C) is considered in children with primary enuresis by the age of 7.
While it may help with enuresis symptoms, it is not appropriate to start this medication
before important investigations are completed.
→ Use of alarm devices (choice D) is also incorrect, as the child’s condition needs to be
properly investigated first.
→ Kidneys, ureters, bladder X-ray (choice E) is incorrect. Despite its name, it is not
typically used to investigate pathology of the kidney, ureter, and bladder. These structures
are better assessed with intravenous pyelogram or CT urography. KUB is typically used to
investigate gastrointestinal conditions such as a bowel obstruction and gallstones, and can
detect the presence of kidney stones.

text:
During rounds, you notice a new rash on a full-term 2-day-old white female. It consists of 1
mm pustules surrounded by a flat area of erythema, and is located on the face, trunk, and
upper arms. An examination is otherwise normal, and she does not appear ill.
Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale:
This infant has the typical “flea-bitten” rash of erythema toxicum neonatorum (ETN). ETN
is a benign self-limited eruption occurring primarily in healthy newborns in the early
neonatal period. Erythema toxicum neonatorum is characterized by macular erythema,
papules, vesicles, and pustules, and it resolves without permanent sequelae.→ Transient neonatal pustular melanosis (choice B) is most common in black newborns,
and the lesions lack the surrounding erythema typical of ETN.
→ Acne neonatorum (choice C) is associated with closed comedones, mostly on the face.
→ As the infant described is not ill, infectious etiologies (choice D and choice E) are
unlikely.

text: Which one of the following is true concerning Norwalk virus?
options:
Outbreaks occur mostly in settings with large numbers of children, such as schools and
day-care centers
Viral shedding continues long after the acute illness
The virus does not survive long on most environmental surfaces
An episode of Norwalk gastroenteritis leads to long-lasting immunity
It is a less common cause of diarrhea in adults than Shigella
rationale:
Outbreaks of Norwalk gastroenteritis occur in a wide variety of settings, involve all ages,
and are more likely to involve high-risk groups such as immunocompromised patients or the
elderly (choice A is incorrect).
Not only does viral shedding of the Norwalk virus often precede the onset of illness, but it
can continue long after the illness has clinically ended (choice B is correct).
The virus persists on environmental surfaces and can tolerate a broad range of temperatures
(choice C is incorrect).
There are multiple strains of the virus, so a single infection does not confer immunity, and
repeated infections occur throughout life (choice D is incorrect).
It is the most common cause of diarrhea in adults (choice E is incorrect).

text:
A 4-year-old female patient is brought to you by her parents on account of having knee pain
over the past few days. The mother says she noticed the girl started limping 2 days ago,
referring pain in her left knee and also had fever, which was not controlled by paracetamol.
She refers that the girl has been irritable, has not been eating well, and she is not as happy as
she usually is. She reports no relevant medical history.
On examination, she has a temperature of 38.7°C, a heart rate of 123 bpm, and a respiratory
rate of 23 /minute. You notice a markedly swollen, red, tender, painful and warm left knee,
which has very limited and painful mobility and no other remarkable signs.
Which of the following diagnostic tests is the best for excluding septic arthritis as a
diagnosis?
options: WBC count of the synovial fluid
rationale:
ESR and CRP (choice B) together have a negative predictive value of almost 90 percent. Of
these, the one with the greatest negative predictive value by it self is CRP. This means that
negative results in CRP (usually less than 1mg/dL) and ESR (less than 20 mm/hr) mean that
the patient is very unlikely to have septic arthritis. Also, CRP is better for monitoring
response to treatment of septic arthritis than other methods.
→ The blood culture (choice A) of a patient with septic arthritis only turns out to be positive
in 40-50 percent of the cases, giving it a very poor negative predictive value.
→ Gram stain of synovial fluid (choice C) is not reliable for the diagnosis or exclusion of
septic arthritis. 50 percent of synovial fluid aspirations are sterile in cases of septic arthritis
confirmed with clinical and laboratory findings, including positive blood culture.
→ Generally speaking, synovial fluid WBC counts (choice D) of more than 50 000 cells/
microL with a predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes indicates a greater likelihood
of the patient having septic arthritis. However, the synovial fluid WBC count is neither
sensitive nor specific for the diagnosis of septic arthritis. It may happen to be much lower in
unusual causes of bacterial arthritis (eg. Brucella), and it may exceed 50 000 cells/microL in
patients with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, serum sickness, or reactive arthritis.
→ Normal X-ray (choice E) does not exclude the diagnosis of Septic Arthritis, therefore it
has a poor negative predictive value. It does not add much to the diagnostic evaluation of Septic Arthritis. However, it may be a valuable adjunct to the examination of the hip, mainly
to compare the contralateral joint.

text:
Over the last 6 months a developmentally normal 12-year-old white female has experienced
intermittent abdominal pain, which has made her quite irritable. She also complains of joint
pain and general malaise. She has lost 5 kg (11 lb) and has developed an anal fissure.
Which one of the following is the most likely cause of these symptoms?
rationale:
The most common age of onset for inflammatory bowel disease is during adolescence and
young adulthood, with a second peak at 50-80 years of age. The manifestations of Crohn’s
disease are somewhat dependent on the site of involvement, but systemic signs and
symptoms are more common than with ulcerative colitis. Perianal disease is also common in
Crohn’s disease. Irritable colon and other functional bowel disorders may mimic symptoms
of Crohn’s disease, but objective findings of weight loss and anal lesions are extremely
uncommon. This is also true for viral hepatitis and giardiasis. In addition, the historical and
epidemiologic findings in this case are not consistent with either of these infections. Celiac
disease and giardiasis can produce Crohn’s-like symptoms of diarrhea and weight loss, but
are not associated with anal fissures.

text: For a healthy 1-month-old, daily vitamin D intake should be:
rationale:
It is now recommended that all infants and children, including adolescents, have a minimum
daily intake of 400 IU of vitamin D, beginning soon after birth. The current
recommendation replaces the previous recommendation of a minimum daily intake of 200
IU/day of vitamin D supplementation beginning in the first 2 months after birth and
continuing through adolescence. These revised guidelines for vitamin D intake for healthy
infants, children, and adolescents are based on evidence from new clinical trials and the
historical precedent of safely giving 400 IU of vitamin D per day in the pediatric and
adolescent population. New evidence supports a potential role for vitamin D in maintaining
innate immunity and preventing diseases such as diabetes mellitus and cancer.

text:
A 15-year-old female is brought to the hospital by her mother because she has never had
menstrual periods and the mother is concerned. On physical examination the girl appears
short, has a webbed neck. Four-limb blood pressures were also evaluated: higher blood
pressures were noted in the arms while the ones of the lower extremities were normal.
Which of the following is the best way to confirm this girl’s diagnosis?
rationale: The source key identifies Karyotype as the best answer.

text:
A 6-year-old girl was brought to your department for follow-up regarding her bed-wetting.
She has never been dry during her night time sleeping. She bed-wets about 3 times a week,
and her bed-wetting history does not include daytime bedwetting. Parents deny any
significant changes in the family or stressful events in their household. Urinalysis, imaging
studies of the urinary system, and the spinal cord evaluation did not reveal any
abnormalities. Which of the following is the best recommendation as next step in
management?
options: Emotional support, diary, and reward system
Reasonable punitive measures for wet nights
rationale: The source key identifies Emotional support, diary, and reward system as the best answer.

text:
A 5-year-old is brought to your department because of fever and headaches. He has had
these symptoms for the last 48 hours and initially parents gave him Tylenol but he seems to
be getting worse. The child’s immunization scheduled was not properly followed. His vital
signs are: temperature 39.9°C, blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, pulse 100 bpm, and
respirations 19/min.
On physical examination he has no petechial rashes, his skin is warm, and nuchal rigidity is
noted. CSF studies reveal elevated neutrophil count, elevated protein, and decreased
glucose. Which of the following is the most common complication to be evaluated on his 6-
week-treatment follow-up appointment?
rationale:
This child’s symptoms of fever, headache, and the findings on physical examination of
nuchal rigidity are suggestive of meningitis. The CSF studies with elevated neutrophil,
increased protein, and decreased glucose point to bacterial meningitis. Children who are not
properly immunized are particularly at risk. Bacterial meningitis can have serious sequelae
even after appropriate treatment. Sensorineural hearing loss (choice C) is noted in 20% to
30% of Hemophilus influenza meningitis survivors. Audiologic assessments are
recommended in these patients in 4 to 6 weeks after antibiotic treatment clears the infection.
There are other possible complications such as hydrocephalus, cortical blindness, epilepsy,
behavioral changes, motor coordination, and intellectual disability; however, the most
common complication that should be assessed 6 weeks after treatment is hearing loss.
→ Subdural effusions (choice A) are asymptomatic complications that generally resolve
without neurological sequelae.
→ Rheumatic heart disease (choice B) occurs as a complication of group A Streptococcus
pharyngitis. It is unlikely to be the cause of meningitis in children of this age. The most
common causes are Pneumococcus pneumonia, Meningococcal meningitis, and Hemophilus
influenza.
→ Cortical blindness (choice D) is a rare complication of meningitis. It is far less common
than hearing loss.
→ Post-infection glomerulonephritis (choice E) is not known to be a complication of the
major bacteria associated with meningitis in children of this age. It can occur in children
with group A streptococcus.

text:
An 8-year-old boy is brought to your department with complaints of hip pain for the last 5
days. The pain is described as constant in nature and has been gradually increasing as it
started out mild but it is getting more severe.
Vital signs are 39°C, BP 110/70 mmHg, pulse 95 bpm, respirations 18/min. Physical
examination reveals focal point tenderness of the proximal femur region. Technetium
radionuclide scan reveals increased osteoblastic activity of proximal femur. Needle
aspiration is performed and the specimen is sent for culture. Which of the following should
be offered as initial treatment at this point?
rationale:
This patient’s clinical picture is suggestive of osteomyelitis. It is suggested by symptoms of
hip pain, fever, tenderness of proximal femur on physical examination, and technetium
radionuclide scan that demonstrates increased osteoblastic activity. It is an inflammation of
the bone primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus though cases of Kingella kingae in
children younger than 3 years of age have been increasing. Bone infections in children are
primarily hematogenous in origin, although cases secondary to penetrating trauma, surgery,
or infection in a contiguous site are also reported.
Initial treatment in this patient would be empirical as the results of bacterial culture have not
yet been obtained. IV vancomycin (choice B) is considered the best initial therapy as it has
adequate coverage against methicillin-resistant staphylococcus.
→ IV nafcillin (choice A) is inappropriate for empiric treatment because of high resistance
rate, estimated to be 30%.
→ IV ciprofloxacin (choice B) would be effective against Kingella kingae, but not against
Staphylococcus aureus. For younger children, fluoroquinolones are also known to cause
cartilaginous tissue damage.→ IV doxycycline (choice D) is inappropriate in children who are 8 years old and younger
due to its adverse effects on teeth. Currently, there’s no sufficient data to support its
effectiveness against methicillin resistant staphylococcus.
→ IV ceftriaxone (choice E) might be helpful in a child with sickle cell anemia who might
have Salmonella or Haemophilus influenza, but is not the best choice in this patient who is
more likely to be infected with Staphylococcus aureus.

text:
As part of a strategy to prevent development of iron deficiency anemia in children, a
regional hospital is planning to do some lab investigations for iron status on blood collected
from children with normal hemoglobin levels for other purposes.
Which of the following lab results marks the most advanced stage of iron deficiency?
options: High serum total iron binding capacity
rationale:
High free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (choice A) marks the most advanced stage of iron
deficiency and indicates that iron deficiency anemia is imminent. Heme synthesis requires
presence of protoporphyrin and iron and when there is no enough of available iron, free
erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) levels rise and hemoglobin synthesis is impaired. If
proper measures to provide iron are not taken, then iron deficiency anemia will develop.The correct sequence of events towards development of iron deficiency anemia is as
follows:
→ Stage 1: Low iron stores: reflected by low serum ferritin (choice E). Despite the low iron
stores, enough iron is transported to the bone marrow to form enough red cells and
hemoglobin stays within the normal range.
→ Stage 2: When iron stores fall further, low serum iron results (choice C). Despite the low
serum iron, however, the rate of hemoglobin synthesis may remain normal. One possible
reason for this is an increased iron extraction capability of developing red cells possibly due
to increased expression of transferrin receptor.
→ Stage 3: The falling serum iron level (choice C) stimulates transferrin synthesis and a rise
of serum transferrin. The low serum iron together with high serum transferrin increase total
iron binding capacity (choice B) and decrease transferrin saturation (choice D).
→ Stage 4: When iron stores are totally depleted, serum iron drops to very low levels,
availability of iron for hemoglobin synthesis will then be compromised. Free erythrocyte
protoporphyrin levels will thus, rise (choice A).

text:
A 15-year-old white male is brought to your department by his mother because he has been waking up at night "drenched
in sweat". This usually occurs between midnight and 1 am and he goes to bed at 10 pm every night. He also reports that
his pre-breakfast blood glucose (at 6 am) is 12.2 mmol/L (220 mg/dL). He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus
and it is treated with insulin. He takes his insulin therapy as prescribed. An hour or so before bedtime he takes 100 units of
insulin, (70 units NPH insulin and 30 units of insulin aspart). What is the best recommendation to manage this patient’s
condition?
options: Reduce the evening dose of insulin by half
Replace NPH and insulin aspart with glargine
Double the dose of NPH and insulin aspart
No change in treatment, eat some sugar if sweating develops in the night
rationale:
This patient is complaining of nights sweats few hours after taking NPH and insulin aspart mix and his morning fasting
glucose levels are 12.2 mmol/L (220 mg/d). Morning hyperglycemia in diabetic patients may be caused by the dawn
phenomenon or the Somogyi’s effect, or simply poor glycemic control.
The dawn phenomenon is associated with physiological (or pathological) decreased insulin secretion in the early morning
hours, accompanied by increase of counterregulatory hormones, particularly the growth hormone. It can occur in patients
with type 1 diabetes mellitus and type 2 diabetes mellitus. On the other hand, the Somogyi’s effect seems to be most
associated with type 1 diabetes and its incidence is increased in young people who take NPH insulin. Hyperglycemia is
usually preceded by hypoglycemia few hours earlier due to the effects of insulin treatment and this could be symptomatic
or asymptomatic. This patient’s night time excessive sweating is most likely caused by hypoglycemia. It has been
observed that in these patients the symptoms are not linked to the level of serum glucose itself as much as to the abrupt
drop of it. A patient whose serum glucose dramatically falls from 5.6 mmol/l (100 mg/dl) to 3.3 mmol/l (60 mg/dl) in an
hour is more likely to be symptomatic than a patient whose serum glucose level gradually decreases from 5.6 mmol/l (100
mg/dl) to 3.3 mmol (45 mg/dl) over 24 hours.
For patients on NPH insulin treatment, hypoglycemic events can be connected with the evident peak of its concentration,
taking place 4-5 hours after evening injections. The best recommendation to manage Somgyi's effect is to replace NPH
insulin with a peakless long-acting analogue such as glargine or detemir (choice C).
→ Nocturnal hormonal measurements (choice A) have shown that patients with morning hyperglycemia have increased
counterregulatory hormones, with growth hormone and glucagon being the most significant and consistent. This patient's
condition is rather obvious and it's more appropriate to change from NPH insulin to long acting insulin than perform more
diagnostic studies.
→ Reduce the evening dose of insulin by half (choice B) is incorrect. In patients treated with NPH insulin who present
with hypoglycemia and Somogyi’s effect, the best treatment is switching to peakless long-acting insulin such as glargine
or detemir; however, if, for some reason, NPH insulin must be used, an alternative is to subtract 2 units from 10 units and
use 8 units. Studies have shown that too rapid reduction in insulin dose can cause persistent severe hyperglycemia and
ketonuria.
→ Double the dose of NPH and insulin aspart (choice D) is incorrect. This reasoning is based on the wrong assumption,
that the patient is not receiving enough insulin treatment but the symptoms of hypoglycemia he experiences in the night
suggest the contrary.
→ No change in treatment, eat some sugar if sweating develops in the night (choice E) is incorrect. This management has
been associated with even higher and longer-lasting morning hyperglycemia.

rationale: Nebulized epinephrine improves moderate-to-severe croup rapidly, but its clinical effect fades after about two hours. text: At an 18-month visit, a boy has a unilateral palpable testis in the inguinal canal that cannot be brought into and remain in the scrotum. There is no hypospadias. What is the most appropriate management?

Begin hormonal therapy to induce descent
Refer promptly for surgical assessment and orchidopexy
Perform orchiectomy because the child is older than 12 months
rationale: Spontaneous descent after six months of corrected age is unlikely. Canadian urology guidance recommends referral by six months and orchidopexy between six and 18 months. Imaging before specialist assessment is usually unnecessary and can be misleading. Hormonal treatment is not recommended as routine primary therapy. At 18 months, further observation delays treatment.

text: A 7-year-old presents with acute fever and severe sore throat. Which finding most strongly supports group A streptococcal pharyngitis rather than a viral illness?
rationale: Canadian Paediatric Society guidance describes GAS pharyngitis as fever, moderate-to-severe sore throat, very tender anterior cervical nodes, absence of cough or rhinorrhea, and inflamed or purulent tonsils. Viral features such as cough, rhinorrhea, conjunctivitis, hoarseness, or oral ulcers lower the likelihood of GAS. Clinical findings guide testing but do not reliably confirm GAS on their own; use a throat swab when testing is indicated.

text: A previously healthy 7-month-old has rhinorrhea, cough, diffuse wheeze and crackles, mild tachypnea, and an oxygen saturation of 94% on room air. The infant is taking smaller feeds but has no apnea and no signs of exhaustion. The presentation is consistent with bronchiolitis. Which is the most appropriate routine management?
options: Support hydration and nasal clearance, monitor clinically, and provide oxygen only if indicated
Start scheduled salbutamol and continue it until wheeze resolves
Give oral dexamethasone for five days
Prescribe an antibiotic for all infants with wheeze
Obtain a chest CT before deciding on treatment
rationale: For otherwise healthy infants with typical bronchiolitis, care is mainly supportive. Assess feeding, hydration, respiratory effort and oxygenation. Routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and advanced imaging do not improve the usual uncomplicated course.

text: A 6-month-old with a first episode of typical bronchiolitis has wheeze but normal perfusion and no history suggesting asthma. Which statement about salbutamol is most accurate?
options: A routine salbutamol trial is recommended because wheeze proves bronchospasm
Salbutamol should be started with every feed to prevent admission
Salbutamol is not routinely recommended when the diagnosis of bronchiolitis is clear
Salbutamol should replace oxygen when saturation falls
Salbutamol is required before nasal suctioning
rationale: In bronchiolitis, small-airway obstruction and edema predominate. Canadian Paediatric Society guidance notes that salbutamol has not improved oxygen saturation, admission rates or length of stay in clear bronchiolitis, so a routine trial is not recommended.

text: A 9-year-old with known asthma presents with marked work of breathing, difficulty speaking in full sentences, an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air, and a PRAM score of 8. Which initial emergency-department plan is most appropriate?
options: Provide oxygen, repeated inhaled salbutamol plus ipratropium, early systemic corticosteroid, and urgent reassessment
Give an oral antihistamine and observe without bronchodilator therapy
Start an antibiotic and wait for a chest radiograph before treating wheeze
Use a long-acting beta agonist alone as immediate rescue therapy
Discharge after one puff of salbutamol because the child is school-aged
rationale: This is a severe exacerbation. Canadian Paediatric Society pathways prioritize oxygen to maintain saturation at or above 92%, frequent short-acting beta2-agonist therapy, ipratropium with initial severe treatments, and systemic corticosteroids early. Persistent severe distress needs escalation rather than delay for routine investigations.

text: A 12-year-old develops generalized hives, hoarseness, wheeze and dizziness minutes after a wasp sting. What is the most important immediate treatment?
options: Intramuscular epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh
An inhaled corticosteroid and home observation
Wait for serum tryptase before treating
rationale: This is anaphylaxis, not isolated urticaria. Intramuscular epinephrine is the life-saving first-line treatment. Antihistamines do not treat airway or circulatory compromise. Emergency assessment and observation are needed because symptoms can recur after initial improvement.

text: A 3-year-old has 16 hours of ear pain, a temperature of 38.2°C, mild tympanic-membrane bulging, and is alert and comfortable after ibuprofen. The family has reliable access to follow-up. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Provide analgesia and use a 24- to 48-hour observation period, with antibiotics if symptoms worsen or fail to improve
Order a CT of the temporal bones before providing pain control
rationale: Mild illness with low-grade fever, mild otalgia and reliable follow-up can be managed with analgesia and watchful waiting. Canadian Paediatric Society guidance recommends antibiotics if symptoms worsen or do not improve within 24 to 48 hours. More severe illness needs a different threshold.

text: An 8-year-old has sore throat, fever, tender anterior cervical nodes, no cough, and a positive rapid test for group A streptococcus. There is no penicillin allergy. Which treatment is recommended?
options: No treatment because all GAS pharyngitis is viral
rationale: For laboratory-confirmed GAS pharyngitis in a child without type-I penicillin allergy, penicillin or amoxicillin for 10 days remains first-line. Macrolides are reserved for selected true anaphylactic beta-lactam allergy because resistance can occur.

text: A 2-year-old has a barky cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor consistent with viral croup. Which therapy should be part of management for children presenting to the emergency department with croup symptoms?
options: Scheduled salbutamol as the primary treatment
No medication because croup is viral
rationale: Corticosteroids are the mainstay treatment for croup. Nebulized epinephrine is added for moderate to severe obstruction, with observation after it is given. Antibiotics and salbutamol do not treat the upper-airway edema of croup.

text: A well-appearing 38-day-old has a documented rectal temperature of 38.2°C and is feeding somewhat less than usual. What is the most appropriate general management setting?
options: Evaluate in a setting able to perform age-appropriate investigation and management for febrile infants up to 90 days
Advise home observation only because the infant looks well
Treat as a routine preschool fever without further assessment
Wait for a rash before considering an evaluation
Give an antipyretic and reassess by telephone next week
rationale: Canadian Paediatric Society guidance states that febrile infants 90 days or younger should be managed where appropriate evaluation and investigations can be performed. Well appearance lowers some risks but does not remove the age-specific pathway.

sub: Temperature assessment in a young infant
text: A parent reports that a 25-day-old felt warm and had a temporal temperature of 38.0°C. The infant is brought for assessment. What should be included in the initial evaluation?
options: A complete history and examination with vital signs, including a rectal temperature measurement
No examination if the temporal temperature is not repeated
Only an ear examination because fever in young infants is usually benign
Delay vital signs until blood results return
rationale: All febrile infants 90 days or younger should receive a complete history and physical examination, including vital signs and rectal temperature assessment. The rectal measurement is central to an age-specific evaluation.

text: A 14-month-old has a rectal temperature of 39.4°C for two days. Examination shows no respiratory, gastrointestinal, skin, or ear source. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Urinalysis, followed by a properly collected urine culture if the urinalysis is not completely normal
No investigation because urinary symptoms cannot be reported
rationale: In children two to 36 months old, fever above 39°C without another source should prompt assessment for UTI. Start with urinalysis and obtain a reliable culture specimen when the urinalysis is not completely normal.

sub: Urinary symptoms in an older child
text: A toilet-trained 7-year-old develops dysuria, urinary frequency, and new daytime incontinence without vaginal irritation. What is the best diagnostic step?
options: Collect a bag specimen for culture
Obtain a midstream urine sample for urinalysis and culture
rationale: Dysuria, frequency, hematuria, abdominal or back pain, and new daytime incontinence support testing for UTI in an older child. A toilet-trained child should provide a midstream urine specimen.

text: A 10-month-old with unexplained fever has a urine bag applied. Which use of the specimen is appropriate?
options: A positive bag culture definitively diagnoses UTI
Use it for culture after antibiotics begin
Use it to select long-term prophylaxis
Bag culture is more reliable than catheter culture
Use it for screening urinalysis, but confirm an abnormal result with catheterization or suprapubic aspiration for culture
rationale: Bag urine is convenient for urinalysis but has a high contamination rate and should not establish UTI by culture. An abnormal screen requires a reliable culture specimen.

text: A non-toilet-trained 18-month-old needs a urine culture before antibiotics. Which collection method is reliable for diagnosis?
options: Any bag specimen with bacterial growth
rationale: For culture in a non-toilet-trained child, urethral catheterization and suprapubic aspiration are reliable diagnostic collection methods. Contaminated methods promote false diagnosis and unnecessary treatment.

text: A febrile 2-year-old is stable but likely has pyelonephritis. When should the urine specimen for urinalysis and culture be obtained?
rationale: An effective antibiotic dose can rapidly sterilize urine. When feasible, obtain urinalysis and culture before starting therapy so the diagnosis and susceptibilities can be assessed.

text: A catheterized urine specimen from a febrile toddler is nitrite positive. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: This replaces the need for culture
rationale: A positive nitrite result is highly specific and makes UTI very likely, though culture is still needed. Nitrite may be falsely negative with frequent voiding or non-nitrate-reducing organisms.

text: A well-appearing 20-month-old with fever has negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite, with no pyuria or bacteriuria on microscopy. What is the best interpretation?
options: The probability of UTI is very low
rationale: When dipstick is negative for leukocyte esterase and nitrite and microscopy shows neither pyuria nor bacteriuria, UTI is very unlikely in the population addressed by the CPS statement.

text: A bag urine culture in an afebrile toddler grows three bacterial species, and urinalysis shows no pyuria. What is the most likely interpretation?
rationale: Mixed growth, low colony counts, absence of pyuria, and a bag specimen all make contamination more likely than true UTI. The diagnosis should not be built on this culture.

text: A 3-year-old with a confirmed febrile UTI is nontoxic, hydrated, has no known urinary abnormality, and can reliably take medication. What is the best initial route of therapy?
options: Mandatory intravenous therapy for every febrile UTI
rationale: Oral antibiotics can be initial treatment for febrile UTI when the child is not seriously ill, has no other admission indication, and can receive and tolerate each dose.

text: A 4-year-old has culture-confirmed febrile UTI and improves promptly on a susceptible oral antibiotic. What treatment duration best reflects CPS guidance?
rationale: CPS recommends seven to 10 days of antibiotic therapy for febrile UTI in infants and children covered by the statement.

text: Empiric therapy was started for a febrile UTI. Culture confirms a pathogen susceptible to a narrower agent. What is the best antibiotic principle?
options: Continue the broadest agent regardless of results
Modify to the narrowest practical effective therapy
Use local resistance patterns only after treatment ends
rationale: Empiric choice should reflect local susceptibility patterns, then therapy should be narrowed when culture and susceptibility results permit.

text: A child was started empirically on antibiotics, but the final culture is mixed growth from a contaminated specimen and the urinalysis was normal. The child is well. What is the best next step?
options: Reassess the diagnosis and stop antibiotics if UTI is unlikely
rationale: When final investigations do not support UTI, the working diagnosis must be revisited and unnecessary antibiotics stopped rather than preserving an unsupported label.

text: A 5-year-old receiving appropriate oral therapy for febrile UTI remains febrile after 48 hours and now has poor urine flow. What is the best next step?
options: Assess for complicated UTI, obtain renal/bladder ultrasound, and use intravenous therapy while clinically indicated
Assume viral illness because antibiotics failed
rationale: Poor urine flow and failure of fever to trend down within 48 hours are complicated-UTI features. Evaluate for obstruction or abscess, usually beginning with renal/bladder ultrasound, and escalate therapy.

text: A 15-month-old recovers from a first well-documented febrile UTI. Which imaging plan is recommended?
options: Renal and bladder ultrasound during or within about two weeks of the illness
rationale: Children younger than two years should have renal/bladder ultrasound after their first febrile UTI to identify significant renal abnormalities, obstruction, or clues to high-grade reflux.

text: A 13-month-old has a first febrile UTI and a normal renal/bladder ultrasound. What is the best next imaging step?
options: No routine VCUG after this first episode with a normal ultrasound
rationale: VCUG is not routinely indicated after the first febrile UTI when renal/bladder ultrasound is normal. This avoids unnecessary radiation and discomfort.

text: After a first febrile UTI, renal/bladder ultrasound shows hydronephrosis and findings concerning for obstruction or high-grade vesicoureteral reflux. What is the best next plan?
options: Order no further assessment because fever resolved
rationale: An ultrasound suggesting high-grade reflux, selected renal anomalies, or obstruction changes the pathway. VCUG and pediatric urology or nephrology input may be indicated.

text: A 20-month-old has a second well-documented febrile UTI after a previous normal ultrasound. Which investigation is now usually indicated?
options: VCUG to assess vesicoureteral reflux and urinary anatomy
rationale: In a child younger than two years, a second well-documented febrile UTI usually warrants VCUG to assess for reflux and urinary tract anatomy.

text: A 9-month-old has completed treatment for a first febrile UTI and is awaiting renal/bladder ultrasound. What is the best prophylaxis plan?
options: Start routine daily antibiotics while waiting
Do not routinely prescribe prophylaxis pending initial ultrasound
Use prophylaxis only after a negative culture
rationale: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended merely while awaiting the initial ultrasound after a first febrile UTI.

text: A postpubertal girl has dysuria and frequency without fever, flank pain, or systemic illness. Culture confirms susceptible uncomplicated lower UTI. Which duration is generally adequate?
options: Two to four days of an appropriate oral antibiotic
No treatment because fever is absent
rationale: Afebrile cystitis is a lower-tract infection. CPS guidance notes that a two- to four-day oral course based on local susceptibility is usually adequate for older children.

sub: UTI in an infant under two months
text: A 5-week-old has documented fever and a urinalysis concerning for UTI. What is the safest management principle?
options: Apply the routine older-child cystitis pathway
Use an age-specific febrile-infant sepsis evaluation rather than the >2-month UTI pathway
Treat only if urinary symptoms are verbalized
Wait for renal ultrasound before assessment
Use a bag culture as the definitive test
rationale: The CPS UTI statement applies to children older than two months. A febrile infant younger than two months needs an age-specific evaluation that considers invasive bacterial infection and sepsis.

text: An 8-year-old with known asthma arrives wheezing and short of breath. Which assessment should be documented now and repeated after treatment?
options: A consistent severity assessment including vital signs, pulse oximetry, air entry, wheeze, and accessory-muscle use
One peak-flow value regardless of technique
rationale: CPS recommends rapid objective severity assessment and use of the same parameters after treatment and at discharge. Pulse oximetry should be used in all patients; PRAM is a validated Canadian tool.

text: A child with an acute asthma exacerbation has a PRAM score of 6. How should this episode be classified?
rationale: PRAM classifies scores 0–3 as mild, 4–7 as moderate, and 8–12 as severe.

text: A 10-year-old with asthma becomes drowsy, has minimal bilateral air entry, and no longer produces an audible wheeze. What is the best interpretation?
options: Impending respiratory failure requiring resuscitation-room care
rationale: A silent chest, minimal air entry, and altered consciousness are life-threatening signs requiring immediate ABC-focused treatment and early critical-care involvement.

text: A 7-year-old with an asthma exacerbation has SpO2 89% on room air. Which oxygen strategy is most appropriate?
options: Give oxygen urgently and aim for at least about 92% to 94%
rationale: CPS recommends urgent oxygen for SpO2 below 92%; at least 92% to 94% is an adequate target while definitive treatment proceeds.

text: A stable 6-year-old has a moderate asthma exacerbation. Which inhaled medication is the bronchodilator of choice?
rationale: Inhaled salbutamol is the bronchodilator of choice; dose and frequency follow severity and response.

text: A cooperative 5-year-old with mild-to-moderate acute asthma can use an inhaler with help. Which delivery method is preferred?
options: Metered-dose inhaler with an age-appropriate spacer
rationale: An MDI with spacer is preferred in almost all non–impending-failure situations because it delivers bronchodilator efficiently with fewer systemic effects.

text: A child has a severe exacerbation and is receiving repeated inhaled salbutamol. Which adjunct should be added during initial treatments?
rationale: Adding ipratropium during the first 60–90 minutes of a moderate-severe or severe crisis improves lung function and reduces admissions; it is not a routine discharge drug.

text: A 9-year-old has a PRAM score of 5. Which anti-inflammatory treatment should be started early?
options: An oral systemic corticosteroid, ideally within the first hour
rationale: Moderate-to-severe exacerbations should receive systemic corticosteroids early, preferably orally and within the first hour, reducing admission and relapse.

text: A child with severe asthma is vomiting and not responding to initial inhaled therapy. What is the best corticosteroid route?
rationale: Oral therapy is preferred when feasible, but severe asthma with vomiting, poor response, or impending failure warrants IV corticosteroid.

text: A child remains in severe distress after 90 minutes of oxygen, repeated salbutamol with ipratropium, and systemic steroid. Which adjunct is appropriate?
options: IV magnesium sulphate with cardiorespiratory monitoring
rationale: IV magnesium should be considered after incomplete response to conventional therapy in the first 1–2 hours; monitoring is needed for hypotension or bradycardia.

text: A 12-year-old with typical asthma has symmetric wheeze, no fever or chest pain, and improves promptly. What is the best imaging plan?
rationale: Chest radiography is rarely indicated in a typical responding exacerbation; reserve it for complications, alternative pathology, persistent asymmetry, marked hypoxemia, or treatment failure.

text: A child with a typical moderate exacerbation improves and remains alert. What is the best approach to blood-gas testing?
options: Do not order routinely; reserve for failure to improve despite aggressive therapy
Replace serial assessment with one gas
rationale: Blood gases are not routine. With persistent distress, normal or rising CO2 can be ominous because acute asthma usually causes hyperventilation and low CO2.

text: Minutes after eating a cookie, a child develops diffuse urticaria, wheeze, and distress. What is the best immediate medication?
rationale: Respiratory distress with urticaria suggests anaphylaxis. IM epinephrine is immediate first-line treatment; asthma therapies do not replace it.

text: Six hours after corticosteroid and conventional therapy, a child still has PRAM 5 and needs salbutamol every 2 hours. What is the best disposition?
rationale: Admission should be considered when PRAM remains at least 4 after 4–6 hours or bronchodilator remains necessary more often than every 4 hours.

text: After 2 hours of optimized therapy, a child remains in severe distress with PRAM 9. What is the best next disposition step?
options: Contact pediatric emergency/PICU expertise and arrange tertiary transfer
rationale: Persistent PRAM 8–12 after 1–2 hours requires early tertiary pediatric emergency or PICU consultation and transfer planning while intensive treatment continues.

text: Which child best meets CPS discharge criteria after an exacerbation?
options: SpO2 94% room air, PRAM 2 sustained 90 minutes, improved air entry, and expected salbutamol no more than every 4 hours
rationale: Discharge requires room-air SpO2 at least 92%, PRAM 3 or less sustained 1–2 hours, improved air entry, and expected SABA no more than every 4 hours.

text: A 9-year-old is discharged after a moderate exacerbation and required oral steroid for another attack 5 months ago. Which controller plan is indicated?
options: No controller until a third attack
One week of doubled ICS only
rationale: Daily ICS is indicated after a moderate or severe exacerbation when oral corticosteroid was required within the last 12 months.

text: A 4-year-old is discharged after a moderate exacerbation requiring oral steroid. Which preventive plan is recommended?
options: Intermittent high-dose ICS only with colds
rationale: For preschoolers, regular daily ICS is recommended after a moderate or severe exacerbation requiring oral corticosteroid.

text: Before discharge, which intervention best supports safe self-management?
options: Review inhaler-spacer technique and provide a written collaborative action plan
rationale: CPS recommends device teaching, trigger review, and a written action plan explaining home treatment and when and where to seek help.

text: When should asthma control, triggers, symptom recognition, and the action plan be reviewed after discharge?
rationale: Follow-up within 4 weeks permits review of control, triggers, technique, adherence, symptom recognition, and the written action plan.

text: A healthy 7-month-old has 2 days of rhinorrhea and cough followed by a first episode of diffuse wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, and mild retractions. What is the best diagnostic approach?
options: Diagnose bronchiolitis clinically from the history and examination
rationale: Typical bronchiolitis is a clinical diagnosis. A viral prodrome followed by a first episode of wheeze or crackles and variable distress in infancy does not require confirmatory testing.

text: A 14-month-old develops abrupt unilateral wheeze while eating peanuts, without fever, rhinorrhea, or cough beforehand. What is the best interpretation?
rationale: Sudden focal wheeze without a viral prodrome is atypical and should prompt evaluation for an alternative such as foreign-body aspiration.

text: A 9-month-old has typical mild bronchiolitis, SpO2 95% on room air, and adequate feeding. Which investigation plan is most appropriate?
rationale: Routine imaging, blood tests, and viral or bacterial cultures rarely change management and can trigger unnecessary treatment.

text: An infant treated supportively for bronchiolitis develops persistent focal crackles, high fever, and fails to improve. What is the best next investigation?
options: No investigation can ever be used
Daily chest radiographs for all infants
Consider a chest radiograph for an alternate diagnosis
rationale: CXR is selective when diagnosis is unclear, improvement is unexpected, or focal and severe findings suggest another diagnosis such as pneumonia.

text: Which situation most appropriately justifies a viral nasopharyngeal test in bronchiolitis?
options: To prove wheeze is not asthma
For hospital cohorting or when a high-risk result changes management
rationale: Viral testing usually does not alter care. It may be useful for cohorting or selected high-risk patients when the result changes investigation, admission, or treatment.

text: Which infant has the clearest baseline risk for severe bronchiolitis?
options: A healthy 2-year-old with a brief cough
rationale: Age under 3 months and birth before 35 weeks predict hospitalization and severe disease. Significant cardiopulmonary disease and immunodeficiency also raise risk.

text: A 4-month-old has grunting, marked indrawing, and a respiratory rate of 68/min. What is the best disposition?
options: Admit for supportive care and repeated assessment
rationale: Severe distress, including grunting, marked indrawing, or respiratory rate above 60/min, supports admission.

text: A 5-month-old has taken less than one-third of usual feeds, has fewer wet diapers, and caregivers cannot reliably return if breathing worsens. What is the best disposition?
options: Admit because hydration and family coping matter
rationale: Admission decisions include respiratory status, hydration, progression risk, apnea or cyanosis, and the family's ability to cope and access reassessment.

text: A stable infant has typical bronchiolitis. What is the best statement about nebulized epinephrine?
options: Not routine; if tried, continue only with clear improvement
rationale: Evidence is insufficient for routine epinephrine. If an observed ED trial is attempted, ongoing doses are inappropriate without clear clinical improvement.

text: An admitted infant has persistent SpO2 88% on room air. Which oxygen plan is appropriate?
options: Start oxygen and maintain saturation at least 90%
rationale: CPS recommends oxygen when saturation falls below 90%, titrated to maintain at least 90%, alongside serial clinical assessment.

text: A congested infant is breathing 66/min and coughs during feeds. What is the best feeding approach?
options: Pause unsafe oral feeding and provide assisted hydration
rationale: Respiratory rate above 60/min can increase aspiration risk. NG or IV hydration can bridge until oral feeding is safe.

text: An infant cannot maintain oral intake. Which statement about supplemental hydration is correct?
options: Nasogastric and intravenous hydration are both acceptable
Oral feeding must continue despite aspiration risk
rationale: NG and IV hydration are similarly effective. NG placement may require fewer attempts; the route is individualized.

text: An infant requires IV maintenance fluid. Which principle is preferred?
options: Isotonic 0.9% NaCl with 5% dextrose and sodium monitoring
rationale: Use isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% dextrose and monitor serum sodium because of hyponatremia risk.

text: Nasal mucus is interfering with feeding. Which suction strategy is most appropriate?
options: Gentle superficial nasal suction when needed
rationale: Gentle superficial suction may help blocked nares, while deep suctioning has been associated with longer hospitalization.

text: A 6-month-old has a first episode of typical bronchiolitis. Which statement about corticosteroids is correct?
options: Routine systemic or inhaled corticosteroids are not recommended
rationale: Corticosteroids do not meaningfully improve scores, admission rates, or length of stay in routine bronchiolitis.

text: A well-appearing infant has typical bronchiolitis without focal bacterial findings. What is the best antibiotic plan?
options: No antibiotics unless bacterial infection is supported
rationale: Antibiotics do not treat bronchiolitis and are reserved for clear evidence or strong suspicion of a secondary bacterial infection.

text: A resident proposes routine nebulized 3% saline for every admitted infant. What is the best response?
options: Current evidence does not support routine use
rationale: 3% hypertonic saline does not meaningfully reduce length of stay in typical North American care and should not be routine.

text: Which intervention should be avoided as routine treatment for uncomplicated bronchiolitis?
options: Gentle superficial nasal suction when needed
rationale: Chest physiotherapy does not improve clinical scores, hospital stay, or symptom duration.

text: An admitted infant is improving, feeding well, weaning from oxygen, and has no apnea risk. What monitoring is most appropriate?
options: Restart oxygen for every brief dip
Repeated clinical assessment with intermittent saturation checks
rationale: Continuous monitoring may suit high-risk infants early; improving low-risk infants can have intermittent checks plus regular clinical assessment.

text: Which infant is most ready for discharge?
options: Improving breathing, saturation above 90% without oxygen, adequate feeding, and caregivers educated with follow-up
rationale: Discharge requires improved breathing, adequate oxygenation without supplemental oxygen or stable home oxygen, adequate feeding, education, and follow-up.

text: A 20-month-old has a preceding coryzal illness, then develops a barky cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor that is worse at night. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale: The combination of barky cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor after an upper respiratory prodrome is classic for viral croup, most often between 6 months and 3 years.

text: A 4-month-old has a second unusually severe episode of croup-like symptoms. What is the best next approach after initial stabilization?
options: Reassure that recurrence is always typical
Assess for congenital or acquired airway narrowing
rationale: Croup before 6 months, recurrent or prolonged episodes, and unusually severe disease warrant assessment for an alternative or underlying airway disorder.

text: A child with stridor has high fever, a toxic appearance, and little improvement after nebulized epinephrine. Which diagnosis is most concerning?
rationale: High fever, toxicity, and poor response to nebulized epinephrine are red flags for bacterial tracheitis rather than uncomplicated viral croup.

text: A child abruptly develops high fever, dysphagia, drooling, anxiety, and sits leaning forward. There is no barky cough. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale: Sudden high fever, drooling, dysphagia, toxic or anxious appearance, tripod or sniffing posture, and absent barky cough are classic red flags for epiglottitis.

text: A toddler has sudden cough and biphasic stridor immediately after choking on a small toy, with decreased air entry on one side. What is the best interpretation?
rationale: A witnessed choking episode, abrupt symptoms, biphasic stridor, wheeze, or asymmetric air entry should prompt urgent evaluation for foreign-body aspiration.

text: A child has an occasional barky cough, no stridor at rest, and only mild indrawing when upset. How should this episode be classified?
rationale: Mild croup has an occasional barky cough, no or minimal stridor at rest, and no to mild indrawing without distress or lethargy.

text: A 2-year-old has frequent barky cough, easily audible stridor at rest, and visible chest indrawing but remains alert. What is the best severity classification?
rationale: Audible stridor and visible indrawing at rest without major lethargy or cyanosis fit moderate croup.

text: A child with croup becomes drowsy and dusky, with decreasing air entry and stridor that is now quieter than before. What is the best interpretation?
options: The child is ready for discharge
rationale: Quietening stridor can be ominous when accompanied by lethargy, cyanosis, or poor air entry because fatigue reduces airflow and sound.

text: A frightened toddler with croup becomes more stridulous when separated from a parent. What is the best immediate supportive measure?
options: Place alone in a mist tent
Keep the child calm with the caregiver and minimize distress
rationale: Agitation worsens upper-airway obstruction. The child should be kept comfortable, ideally with the caregiver, while assessment and treatment minimize frightening interventions.

text: A child has mild croup. Which statement about humidified air or a mist tent is most accurate?
options: It is required for every case
It is not supported by evidence and mist tents are not recommended
rationale: Humidified air has not shown benefit, and mist tents can separate children from caregivers and disperse fungus; they are not recommended.

text: A child has mild croup with a barky cough but no stridor at rest. Which medication plan is best?
options: Give a single dose of dexamethasone
No corticosteroid unless intubation is needed
Give repeated nebulized epinephrine at home
rationale: Corticosteroids benefit croup across the spectrum from mild to severe and reduce return visits and admissions.

text: Which dexamethasone regimen is best supported by the Canadian Paediatric Society practice point for croup?
rationale: A single dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is the regimen used in most trials and is highly effective; lower-dose equivalence remains less certain.

text: A child with croup is alert, not vomiting, and can swallow. What is the preferred corticosteroid route?
rationale: Oral dexamethasone is preferred because it is as effective as or better than nebulized therapy and is less associated with vomiting. IM dosing is reserved when oral delivery is unreliable.

text: A child with severe croup has persistent vomiting and cannot retain oral medication. What is the best corticosteroid plan?
options: Use an oral dose repeatedly until retained
rationale: IM corticosteroid is appropriate when vomiting or significant respiratory distress makes oral administration unreliable.

text: After oral dexamethasone for croup, which expected time course should guide counselling?
options: It works fully in 2 minutes and lasts 1 hour
It has no effect until 3 days
It must be repeated every hour
Improvement generally begins in 2–3 hours and persists 24–48 hours
rationale: Dexamethasone is not an instant rescue drug; improvement usually starts within 2 to 3 hours and lasts 24 to 48 hours.

text: A toddler has stridor and indrawing at rest from moderate croup. Which treatment should be added to dexamethasone?
rationale: Nebulized epinephrine is recommended for moderate to severe croup because it rapidly reduces upper-airway obstruction while steroid benefit develops.

text: A child improves 15 minutes after nebulized epinephrine. Why is continued observation required?
options: Epinephrine commonly causes delayed bacterial infection
Its clinical effect disappears by about 2 hours, so symptoms may recur
The child must receive routine antibiotics
rationale: Nebulized epinephrine acts within 10 to 30 minutes, but its effect wanes and is gone by approximately 2 hours, so recurrence must be excluded.

text: A child received dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine for moderate croup. Which finding best supports safe discharge?
options: Persistent stridor at rest after 1 hour
No recurrence of croup symptoms during 2–4 hours of observation
A second epinephrine dose was just given
rationale: Discharge is supported when symptoms do not recur during 2 to 4 hours of observation after epinephrine and the child otherwise remains clinically safe.

text: A child with severe croup has poor and unsustained response to dexamethasone and nebulized epinephrine. What is the best next disposition?
options: Routine outpatient review in one month
Urgent paediatric intensive-care or anaesthesia support
rationale: Severe distress or impending respiratory failure with poor or unsustained initial response requires advanced airway expertise and critical-care escalation.

text: A child has typical viral croup and improves after standard therapy. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Heliox is routine for mild disease
Antibiotics and beta-2 agonists are rarely indicated in typical croup
rationale: Typical croup is viral upper-airway disease, so antibiotics and beta-2 agonists are rarely appropriate. Persistent severe symptoms or multiple atypical episodes instead prompt specialty airway assessment.

text: An 18-month-old has acute ear pain and fever. Otoscopy shows a yellow, markedly bulging tympanic membrane with impaired mobility. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rationale: Acute symptoms plus middle-ear effusion and significant inflammation—especially a bulging, yellow or hemorrhagic tympanic membrane—support AOM.

text: A well child has an air-fluid level behind a non-bulging tympanic membrane after a cold, without fever or significant ear pain. What is the best interpretation?
options: Otitis media with effusion without acute inflammation
rationale: Middle-ear fluid without bulging or acute inflammatory findings is OME, not AOM. Air-fluid levels or erythema alone have poor predictive value for AOM.

text: A 3-year-old has acute otalgia followed by purulent otorrhea through a newly perforated tympanic membrane. What is the best management?
options: Start prompt systemic antimicrobial therapy and assess for complications
Treat as uncomplicated otitis externa only
Delay treatment until a culture is positive
rationale: Acute perforation with purulent discharge strongly supports bacterial AOM. CPS recommends prompt systemic antimicrobials and examination for associated complications.

text: A child treated for AOM develops fever, postauricular pain and swelling, and the pinna is displaced outward. What is the best next step?
options: Urgently evaluate for mastoiditis, including systemic therapy and possible imaging or surgery
Wait one month for hearing testing
rationale: Pain or swelling over the mastoid after AOM suggests acute mastoiditis, a spread-beyond-the-middle-ear complication requiring urgent systemic treatment and specialist evaluation.

text: A healthy 4-year-old has mild AOM, temperature 38.1°C, mild otalgia, is alert and drinking, and reliable follow-up is available. What is the best initial plan?
options: Analgesia plus 24–48 hours of observation with reassessment or a delayed prescription
rationale: Mild illness with temperature below 39°C, mild pain, and reliable follow-up can be managed with watchful waiting for 24 to 48 hours and clear safety-netting.

text: Which child with a clearly bulging tympanic membrane most needs immediate antimicrobial therapy?
options: A child with temperature 39.4°C, severe otalgia, and systemic illness
An alert child with mild pain for 6 hours and temperature 37.8°C
A child with asymptomatic residual effusion
A child whose ear exam is normal
rationale: Immediate treatment is recommended with fever at least 39°C, moderate-to-severe systemic illness, severe otalgia, or significant illness lasting 48 hours.

text: A toddler with mild AOM is selected for watchful waiting. Which additional intervention is essential?
options: Appropriate analgesia and caregiver safety-net instructions
No treatment because antibiotics were deferred
rationale: Observation is active management: caregivers need advice on analgesics, what worsening looks like, and how to obtain reassessment within 24 to 48 hours.

text: A 20-kg child needs first-line oral amoxicillin for uncomplicated AOM using twice-daily dosing. Which total daily dose is appropriate?
rationale: Because amoxicillin has a short half-life, twice-daily treatment requires 75 to 90 mg/kg/day to maintain adequate middle-ear concentrations.

text: Which amoxicillin regimen is an accepted first-line alternative when dosing three times daily for AOM?
rationale: CPS lists amoxicillin 45 to 60 mg/kg/day divided three times daily as equivalent first-line dosing to the higher total daily BID regimen.

text: A child has a bulging tympanic membrane and concurrent purulent conjunctivitis. Which empiric oral treatment is preferred?
rationale: Purulent otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome suggests beta-lactamase-producing H influenzae or M catarrhalis, making amoxicillin-clavulanate preferred.

text: A child with definite AOM completed amoxicillin 18 days ago for another infection. Which empiric agent is most appropriate now?
options: Repeat a low dose of amoxicillin
rationale: Amoxicillin exposure within the previous 30 days raises concern for beta-lactamase-producing pathogens; CPS supports amoxicillin-clavulanate.

text: A child needs treatment for AOM and previously developed a delayed, nonurticarial rash with amoxicillin but no angioedema, bronchospasm, or hypotension. What is a reasonable alternative?
options: No antibiotic can ever be used
A second- or third-generation cephalosporin such as cefuroxime
rationale: For a non-life-threatening penicillin reaction, CPS accepts selected second- or third-generation cephalosporins. The allergy history should be characterized carefully.

text: A child requiring AOM treatment had hypotension and bronchospasm immediately after penicillin. Which principle is best?
options: Use cefuroxime without reviewing the reaction
Avoid beta-lactams implicated in a life-threatening reaction and choose a non-beta-lactam option with awareness of inferior coverage
Withhold all treatment despite severe disease
rationale: Life-threatening immediate reactions exclude routine beta-lactam alternatives. Macrolide or clindamycin may be used, although their bacterial killing is generally inferior, so expert input may be needed.

text: A child has persistent pain, fever, and a bulging tympanic membrane after 72 hours of correctly dosed amoxicillin with good adherence. What is the best next antimicrobial?
options: Stop all treatment because effusion persists
rationale: Persistent symptomatic AOM after two to three days of adequate amoxicillin suggests beta-lactamase-producing pathogens or a complication; reassess and change to amoxicillin-clavulanate when persistent AOM is confirmed.

text: A child cannot tolerate oral antibiotics and has persistent AOM after amoxicillin-clavulanate. Which rescue regimen may be considered?
options: Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV daily for three days
rationale: CPS reserves ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg daily for three days for oral intolerance or amoxicillin-clavulanate failure; tympanocentesis or ENT referral may also be considered.

sub: Antibiotic duration age two and older
text: A healthy 5-year-old has uncomplicated AOM and responds promptly to first-line amoxicillin. What treatment duration is recommended?
rationale: Five days is appropriate for most children at least 2 years old with uncomplicated AOM.

text: A 14-month-old requires antimicrobial treatment for confirmed AOM. What is the appropriate usual duration?
rationale: Children 6 to 23 months old should receive a 10-day course when antibiotics are indicated.

text: Which situation in an older child still calls for a 10-day antimicrobial course for AOM?
options: AOM with perforated tympanic membrane, recurrent disease, or initial treatment failure
rationale: Ten days is reserved not only for children under 2, but also for perforated AOM, recurrent AOM, and cases where initial therapy failed.

text: Three weeks after successful AOM treatment, a child is well but still has a middle-ear effusion without bulging, fever, or pain. What is the best antibiotic plan?
options: Do not change antibiotics solely for persistent effusion
rationale: Middle-ear effusion may persist for months after clinical and bacterial resolution. Effusion alone does not indicate treatment failure or a need to change antimicrobials.

text: A child starting amoxicillin for AOM has worsening pain and fever after 48 hours. What is the best next action?
options: Assume this is normal for one week
Wait until the course ends without examination
Treat residual fluid rather than symptoms
Reassess for persistent AOM, adherence, or complications and adjust treatment if confirmed
rationale: Symptoms should improve within 24 hours and resolve over two to three days. Worsening or non-improvement requires reassessment before changing therapy.

text: An 8-year-old develops fever and sore throat in February. Which epidemiologic feature most supports group A streptococcal pharyngitis?
options: Peak occurrence at age 5 to 11 years in winter and spring
Peak occurrence in infants younger than 6 months
Routine bacterial cause of every childhood sore throat
rationale: GAS pharyngitis occurs most often at ages 5 to 11 and is more common in winter and spring; most acute pharyngitis remains viral.

text: A 7-year-old has sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, and no fever. What is the best next step?
options: Manage as likely viral pharyngitis without routine GAS testing
rationale: Cough and rhinorrhea lower the pretest probability of GAS. A positive culture in this setting can represent carriage rather than the cause of symptoms.

text: A 2-year-old has a mild sore throat and rhinorrhea during a family cold. There is no scarlet-fever rash and no outbreak. What is the best approach to GAS testing?
options: Do not routinely test because GAS pharyngitis is rare under age three
Perform a rapid test and treat any positive result
rationale: GAS pharyngitis is rare in children younger than 3 years. CPS limits testing in this age group to outbreak settings or suspected scarlet fever.

text: Which presentation has the highest pretest probability of GAS pharyngitis?
options: Sore throat with cough and rhinorrhea
Fever above 38°C, tender anterior cervical nodes, inflamed exudative tonsils, and no cough
rationale: Fever, moderate-to-severe sore throat, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, inflamed or purulent tonsils, and absence of cough or rhinorrhea characterize GAS pharyngitis.

text: A 10-year-old has fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, and no cough. What is the best next step in a low-ARF-risk community?
options: Treat without testing because the score is diagnostic
Observe without testing despite high probability
Obtain a throat swab for microbiologic confirmation
rationale: A CENTOR score of at least 3 identifies children who warrant a throat swab. The score guides testing, not automatic treatment.

text: Which investigation is the gold standard for confirming GAS pharyngitis?
options: Bacterial culture of a swab from the tonsils and posterior pharyngeal wall
rationale: The gold standard is culture from a properly collected swab of the tonsils and posterior pharyngeal wall.

text: A symptomatic child in a community with a high burden of acute rheumatic fever has a negative rapid antigen detection test. What is the best next step?
options: Confirm the negative rapid test with throat culture
rationale: RADT specificity is high but sensitivity is lower. In high-ARF-burden settings, a negative RADT should be confirmed with culture.

text: A child has an acute sore throat and possible GAS pharyngitis. Why is an anti-streptolysin O titre not the appropriate diagnostic test?
options: It is always negative after GAS
It cannot distinguish GAS carriage from active acute infection
It is more invasive than throat surgery
It becomes positive only with otitis media
rationale: ASO titres reflect an immune response and cannot reliably separate asymptomatic carriage from active acute GAS pharyngitis.

text: A well 9-year-old in a low-ARF-risk community has a positive throat culture after a high-probability presentation. What is the best management?
options: Treat laboratory-confirmed GAS with penicillin or amoxicillin
rationale: In low-risk populations, microbiologic confirmation should precede antibiotics. A positive culture with compatible symptoms should be treated.

text: A child with probable GAS is stable while a throat culture is pending. Which stewardship plan remains safe for preventing acute rheumatic fever?
options: Never treat after the first 24 hours
Treat only if symptoms persist for a month
Use antibiotics only after an elevated ASO titre
Provide a delayed prescription to be filled for a positive culture, ensuring treatment begins within 9 days of symptom onset
rationale: Treatment within 9 days of symptom onset prevents ARF, allowing a delayed prescription linked to a positive culture in a stable child.

text: A 30-kg child has culture-confirmed GAS pharyngitis and no drug allergy. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg once daily, maximum 1 g daily, for 10 days
Azithromycin for 10 days as first choice
rationale: CPS recommends amoxicillin 50 mg/kg once daily, or 25 mg/kg twice daily, to a maximum of 1 g/day for 10 days.

text: A 6-year-old has confirmed GAS pharyngitis, but the family is very unlikely to complete 10 days of oral medication. What is the best alternative?
options: A single weight-based intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G
rationale: For anticipated poor adherence, CPS lists one weight-based intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G as an alternative.

text: A child with confirmed GAS once developed a delayed nonurticarial rash with penicillin and had no anaphylaxis. Which option is most appropriate?
options: Consider an oral amoxicillin challenge or use cephalexin for 10 days
