rationale: For non-anaphylactic reactions, CPS recommends an oral amoxicillin challenge or cephalexin 20 mg/kg/dose twice daily for 10 days.

text: A child with confirmed GAS had documented immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin. Which treatment principle is best?
options: Choose azithromycin, clarithromycin, or clindamycin and check local susceptibility
rationale: Macrolides or clindamycin are options for documented type I hypersensitivity, but regional resistance can reach 20%, so local susceptibility matters.

text: Which adjunct is recommended for pain and fever in uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis?
rationale: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen is recommended for symptom management. Routine corticosteroids are discouraged because evidence quality and safety are concerns.

text: Which complication is not prevented by antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis?
rationale: Antibiotics help prevent ARF and suppurative complications, but they have not been shown to prevent post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

text: A child with repeated positive GAS cultures improves only gradually over 3 days after antibiotics, similar to prior viral episodes. What is the best interpretation?
options: Consider viral pharyngitis with chronic GAS carriage
Every positive culture proves recurrent acute GAS
rationale: True GAS pharyngitis usually improves within 24 hours; slower improvement over 2 to 3 days suggests viral pharyngitis with incidental GAS carriage.

text: A child completed treatment for GAS and is now asymptomatic. What is the best follow-up testing plan?
options: Weekly throat cultures for three months
Do not routinely repeat throat culture unless a special high-risk or outbreak situation applies
rationale: Routine post-treatment cultures and cultures of asymptomatic children are not recommended. Exceptions include certain ARF-risk families, apparent household transmission, or closed-community outbreaks.

text: A 9-year-old with a high CENTOR score lives in a remote community with high ARF burden where neither RADT nor culture is available. What is the best plan?
options: No treatment is permitted without a test
Consider empiric treatment in this select high-risk setting
rationale: In high-ARF-risk settings where testing is unavailable, CPS advises considering empiric therapy for children with higher clinical scores.

text: A child with recent sore throat develops muffled voice, unilateral tonsillar swelling, uvular deviation, and difficulty opening the mouth. What is the best next step?
options: Use a delayed prescription without examination
Urgently assess for peritonsillar abscess and airway or drainage needs
rationale: This is a suppurative deep-space complication rather than uncomplicated pharyngitis and requires urgent airway-aware assessment and source control planning.

text: A previously healthy immunized 4-year-old has radiographically confirmed community-acquired bacterial pneumonia. Which organism should empiric therapy primarily cover?
rationale: Streptococcus pneumoniae remains the predominant bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia in otherwise healthy children of all ages.

text: A 2-year-old has cough, wheeze, diffuse crackles, and a winter viral prodrome without focal consolidation. What is the most likely etiologic category?
rationale: Viruses are the most common causes of pneumonia-like lower respiratory illness in infants and preschool children, especially with diffuse wheeze and a viral prodrome.

text: A calm 18-month-old with fever and cough has a respiratory rate of 44/min. How should this rate be interpreted?
options: Normal because all toddlers may breathe up to 60/min
Tachypnea because the upper limit from age 1 to 5 years is about 40/min
rationale: For children 1 to 5 years old, approximately 40 breaths/min is the upper limit used to define tachypnea; count for a full minute while calm.

text: A child presents to hospital with fever, cough, and increased work of breathing but no visible cyanosis. What bedside test is specifically indicated?
rationale: Hypoxemia may not be clinically apparent, so oxygen saturation should be measured in all hospital presentations or significant illness. Normal saturation does not exclude pneumonia.

text: A toddler has prominent wheeze and hypoxemia after coryza, with no focal percussion or breath-sound abnormality. What diagnosis should be prioritized over bacterial pneumonia?
options: Bronchiolitis or asthma with mucus plugging
rationale: When wheeze and hypoxia predominate without focal consolidation, bronchiolitis or asthma with mucus plugging is more likely than bacterial pneumonia.

text: A stable 7-year-old has fever, focal crackles, bronchial breath sounds, and a classic uncomplicated pneumonia presentation. Oral intake and oxygenation are normal. What is the best imaging plan?
options: A chest radiograph is not essential when clinical suspicion is high and hospitalization is unnecessary
Ultrasound is mandatory in every case
rationale: Although imaging can support diagnosis, a chest radiograph is not essential for a well outpatient with a highly typical history and examination.

text: A 5-year-old is admitted with hypoxemia and suspected pneumonia. Which investigation should be obtained to define disease extent and look for effusion or abscess?
options: No imaging because pneumonia is clinical
rationale: All hospitalized children with suspected pneumonia should have a chest radiograph to assess extent and identify pleural effusion or abscess.

text: A child has a positive respiratory viral test and chest radiograph showing patchy nonconsolidative changes, with no convincing secondary bacterial features. What is the best treatment?
rationale: When findings support viral pneumonia without convincing bacterial superinfection, treatment is supportive, including oxygen and hydration when required.

text: Which child with pneumonia most clearly requires hospital admission?
options: A playful child with normal intake and oxygenation
A school-aged child improving on oral therapy
A child with isolated cough and normal vital signs
A child with grunting, hypoxemia, and inability to maintain oral intake
A child whose fever resolved yesterday
rationale: Respiratory compromise, hypoxemia, inadequate oral intake, intolerance of oral therapy, severe illness, or complicated pneumonia are key admission indications.

text: A 4-month-old has pneumonia but currently appears only moderately ill. Which disposition principle is best?
options: Home care is mandatory if afebrile
Treat only if a culture is positive
Use a lower threshold for hospital admission because subtle deterioration is harder to recognize
rationale: Infants younger than 6 months warrant a lower admission threshold because they may need more support and clinical deterioration can be subtle.

text: A healthy immunized 6-year-old has nonsevere lobar community-acquired pneumonia and can take oral medication. What is the preferred empiric antibiotic?
rationale: Oral amoxicillin is first-line outpatient therapy because it provides appropriate narrow-spectrum pneumococcal coverage.

text: A fully immunized child is hospitalized with bacterial pneumonia but has no shock or respiratory failure. What is the preferred empiric IV treatment?
rationale: IV ampicillin is recommended for hospitalized children with non-life-threatening uncomplicated CAP and preserves narrow pneumococcal coverage.

text: A child with pneumonia develops septic shock and respiratory failure. Which empiric antibiotic approach is most appropriate?
options: A third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime
rationale: Respiratory failure or septic shock requires broader empiric therapy with ceftriaxone or cefotaxime while cultures and stabilization proceed.

text: A critically ill child has rapidly progressive multilobar pneumonia with pneumatoceles. What should be added empirically to a third-generation cephalosporin?
rationale: Rapid multilobar progression or pneumatoceles raises concern for staphylococcal disease, including MRSA, so empiric vancomycin is added until cultures clarify.

text: A 12-year-old has 10 days of malaise and headache followed by persistent cough, mild fever, minimal leukocytosis, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates. What treatment may hasten recovery if illness is significant or persistent?
rationale: This subacute school-age phenotype suggests Mycoplasma or Chlamydophila; a macrolide may be used for more serious illness or persistent cough.

text: A healthy 8-year-old has nonsevere ambulatory bacterial pneumonia and improves promptly on amoxicillin. What treatment duration is supported by the 2024 CPS update?
options: Continue until the radiograph is normal
rationale: Recent evidence supports 5 days for nonsevere ambulatory pneumonia when the child responds appropriately.

text: A hospitalized child on IV ampicillin is now afebrile, off oxygen, eating, and ready for discharge. What is the best antibiotic plan?
options: Continue IV therapy until every opacity resolves
Stop after one inpatient dose regardless of course
rationale: Oral step-down is appropriate once clinical improvement, defervescence, and discharge readiness are achieved.

text: A child receiving appropriate amoxicillin for bacterial pneumonia remains febrile and tachypneic after 72 hours. What is the best next step?
options: Automatically double the dose without assessment
Assume radiographic lag explains all symptoms
Reassess clinically and obtain imaging for empyema, abscess, or an alternate diagnosis
rationale: Failure to improve within 48 to 72 hours requires clinical reassessment and chest radiography or ultrasound to identify complications or another diagnosis.

text: A child with pneumonia has a large pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise and remains febrile despite antibiotics. What is the best next management step?
options: Arrange pleural-fluid culture and drainage with specialist management
rationale: A large or clinically significant effusion, especially with respiratory compromise or poor medical response, requires drainage for therapeutic and diagnostic purposes.

text: Four weeks after uncomplicated pneumonia, a child is asymptomatic with a normal examination. The original radiograph showed lobar consolidation. What is the best follow-up imaging plan?
options: No routine repeat chest radiograph when clinical recovery is complete
rationale: Radiographic clearing can take 4 to 6 weeks. Repeat imaging is not indicated in an otherwise well child who has recovered clinically.

text: A previously healthy 7-year-old presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and altered behaviour. Which Canadian pathway best fits this presentation?
options: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis guidance for children older than 2 months
rationale: The CPS statement applies to previously healthy children older than 2 months with suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis. Neonates, CSF-shunt infections, enteric gram-negative disease, TB, and viral meningoencephalitis require other pathways.

text: A stable 10-year-old has suspected bacterial meningitis and no contraindication to lumbar puncture. Which CSF plan is most appropriate?
options: Cell count, glucose, protein, culture, and molecular testing when indicated
No CSF testing if fever is present
rationale: Definitive evaluation includes CSF cell count, glucose, protein, microbiological culture, and molecular detection when suspicion remains high despite negative cultures; viral or TB studies are added when clinically appropriate.

text: A 6-year-old with suspected meningitis is hypotensive, poorly perfused, and requires active resuscitation. What is the best immediate diagnostic approach?
options: Perform lumbar puncture before any other action
Wait for neck stiffness to resolve
Defer lumbar puncture because shock makes the child clinically unstable
rationale: An unstable clinical state such as shock is a contraindication to immediate lumbar puncture. Stabilization, blood cultures when feasible, and prompt empiric therapy take priority.

text: A child with suspected meningitis has a new focal seizure and reduced consciousness. What is the best next diagnostic sequence?
options: Lumbar puncture immediately regardless of findings
Defer lumbar puncture and obtain urgent neuroimaging to assess herniation risk
Wait for an outpatient MRI next week
rationale: New seizures, focal neurologic deficits, papilledema, or markedly reduced consciousness require deferring LP until urgent neuroimaging has addressed herniation risk.

text: A 9-year-old has suspected meningitis, but urgent CT will delay lumbar puncture. What is the best treatment plan?
options: Withhold antibiotics until CSF is obtained
Wait for a positive blood culture
Obtain blood cultures promptly when feasible and start empiric IV antimicrobials without waiting for imaging or LP
rationale: Timely empiric antimicrobial therapy is critical. Blood cultures should be obtained first when feasible, but imaging or inability to perform LP must not delay antibiotics.

text: A previously healthy 5-year-old has suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis. Cultures are pending. Which empiric regimen is recommended?
options: IV ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus IV vancomycin
rationale: For children older than 2 months with suspected bacterial meningitis, CPS recommends a third-generation cephalosporin plus vancomycin pending blood and CSF results.

text: A 13-year-old receiving intensive immunosuppressive therapy develops suspected bacterial meningitis. What addition to ceftriaxone and vancomycin is appropriate?
rationale: CPS recommends adding ampicillin when an immunocompromised child is at risk for Listeria, while retaining standard empiric meningitis coverage.

text: A child received antibiotics before transfer. Blood and CSF cultures are negative, but the clinical course and CSF profile support bacterial meningitis. Local pneumococcal cephalosporin resistance is not a concern. What regimen is appropriate?
options: Continue ceftriaxone or cefotaxime without vancomycin
rationale: When bacterial meningitis remains supported despite negative cultures, CPS recommends ceftriaxone or cefotaxime; vancomycin can be stopped unless local third-generation cephalosporin resistance warrants continuing it.

text: CSF grows Streptococcus pneumoniae with a meningitis penicillin MIC at or below 0.06 mcg/mL. What is the best definitive treatment?
options: Narrow to IV penicillin G or ampicillin
rationale: A pneumococcal isolate meeting the meningitis-specific penicillin susceptibility breakpoint can be treated with IV penicillin G or ampicillin.

text: A child has pneumococcal meningitis. The isolate is penicillin resistant and ceftriaxone or cefotaxime intermediate or resistant. What is the best treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus vancomycin with infectious-disease consultation
rationale: For pneumococcus with reduced third-generation cephalosporin susceptibility, CPS recommends ceftriaxone or cefotaxime plus vancomycin and specialist consultation.

text: CSF identifies penicillin-susceptible Neisseria meningitidis. Which definitive antimicrobial is appropriate?
rationale: Penicillin-susceptible meningococcal meningitis can be narrowed to IV penicillin G or ampicillin; ceftriaxone or cefotaxime is an alternative.

text: A partially immunized child has Haemophilus influenzae meningitis. The isolate is confirmed ampicillin susceptible. What is the best definitive therapy?
rationale: When H influenzae is confirmed ampicillin susceptible, CPS lists IV ampicillin as definitive therapy.

text: A stable child has suspected bacterial meningitis, and the CSF Gram stain shows gram-negative coccobacilli consistent with H influenzae. What adjunct should be considered?
options: Dexamethasone started with the first antimicrobial dose
No adjunct can ever be considered
rationale: Dexamethasone should be considered when the Gram stain suggests H influenzae, with greatest potential benefit when given immediately before, with, or shortly after the first antimicrobial dose.

text: Dexamethasone was started for a Gram stain suggestive of Hib, but neither culture nor molecular testing identifies Hib within 48 hours. What is the best plan?
options: Delay the decision until audiology testing
rationale: If Hib is not positively identified within 48 hours, CPS recommends discontinuing dexamethasone.

text: A child has presumptive pneumococcal meningitis and dexamethasone is started with antibiotics. Pneumococcus is not identified within 48 hours. What should happen?
options: Repeat LP solely to justify steroids
rationale: Empiric dexamethasone may be considered for presumptive pneumococcal meningitis, but should be stopped if pneumococcus is not identified within 48 hours.

text: Dexamethasone is indicated for a child with bacterial meningitis. Which regimen matches CPS guidance?
options: 0.6 mg/kg/day divided every 6 hours, begun immediately before, with, or within 4 hours of the first antimicrobial
One dose one week after antibiotics
Daily oral steroid for six weeks
Steroid only after hearing loss appears
rationale: CPS recommends dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg/day in four divided doses every 6 hours, begun immediately before, concomitantly with, or within 4 hours of the first antimicrobial; earlier is likely better.

text: A child with pneumococcal meningitis improves promptly on active therapy. The isolate is susceptible and dexamethasone was not used. What is the best repeat-LP plan?
options: Do not routinely repeat CSF sampling
Repeat LP before each antibiotic dose
Replace LP with routine weekly CT
rationale: Repeat CSF sampling is generally unnecessary for common pathogens when the child improves. It is considered when improvement fails, and in selected resistant pneumococcal, steroid-treated pneumococcal, GBS, or enteric gram-negative cases.

text: A child has uncomplicated pneumococcal meningitis and responds normally. What IV treatment duration is recommended?
rationale: Uncomplicated S pneumoniae meningitis is treated with IV antimicrobials for 10 to 14 days.

text: A child has uncomplicated meningococcal meningitis with rapid clinical response. What IV treatment duration is recommended?
rationale: CPS recommends 5 to 7 days of IV antimicrobial therapy for uncomplicated N meningitidis meningitis.

text: A child is recovering after confirmed bacterial meningitis and is nearing discharge. What follow-up must be arranged?
options: Audiology only if a parent notices hearing loss
No hearing assessment after pneumococcal disease
Formal audiology as soon as possible after diagnosis and always before hospital discharge
rationale: All affected children should receive formal audiology assessment as soon as possible after diagnosis and always before discharge so hearing loss can be managed promptly.

text: A 52-day-old infant appears well in the emergency department. A rectal temperature measured at home was 38.1 C. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Fever is present only if the emergency department temperature is at least 38.5 C
The home measurement can be ignored because the infant is now afebrile
A rectal temperature at least 38.0 C at home or in a clinical setting meets the fever definition
Only axillary temperature should guide management
No assessment is needed if feeding is normal
rationale: A documented rectal temperature of at least 38.0 C is fever in an infant 90 days or younger, even if the infant is afebrile on arrival.

sub: Afebrile on arrival after documented fever
text: A 45-day-old infant had a rectal temperature of 38.2 C at home but is 37.4 C on arrival and looks well. What is the best next step?
options: Proceed with age-appropriate evaluation for a febrile young infant
Obtain a chest radiograph without other tests
Repeat the temperature in one week
rationale: Infants with documented fever at home do not have a lower risk simply because they are afebrile at presentation. They require age-based assessment.

text: Which investigation is recommended for every febrile infant aged 90 days or younger?
rationale: Every febrile young infant should have urine assessed for infection. Other tests vary with age, appearance, risk markers, and clinical findings.

text: A urine specimen is needed from a 6-week-old febrile infant. Which collection approach is preferred for culture?
rationale: Catheterization and suprapubic aspiration reduce contamination. Bag specimens are not preferred for culture.

text: A 24-day-old infant is febrile, mottled, lethargic, and poorly perfused. What is the best immediate approach?
options: Complete a lumbar puncture before any other action
Give oral antibiotics and reassess tomorrow
Stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation; obtain cultures and start empiric antibiotics without delay
rationale: An ill-appearing infant requires immediate resuscitation and empiric treatment. Lumbar puncture can wait until the infant is stable.

text: A well-appearing 18-day-old infant has a rectal temperature of 38.0 C. Which initial test set is most appropriate?
options: CBC with differential, inflammatory marker, blood culture, urinalysis, and urine culture
rationale: Febrile infants 0 to 28 days need blood and urine evaluation plus inflammatory markers. CSF evaluation depends on risk and clinical context but is required when high-risk features are present.

text: A well-appearing 20-day-old infant meets validated low-risk criteria. Which disposition is most appropriate?
options: Hospital observation; lumbar puncture is not automatically required
Oral antibiotics at home without cultures
No further assessment because the infant is low risk
rationale: Even low-risk febrile infants 0 to 28 days are hospitalized for observation. Lumbar puncture can be individualized in selected low-risk cases.

text: A well-appearing 40-day-old infant has a positive urinalysis but normal inflammatory markers. What is the best interpretation?
options: The infant may remain low risk for invasive bacterial infection and can receive UTI treatment with reliable follow-up
A positive urinalysis alone proves meningitis
Lumbar puncture is mandatory solely because the urinalysis is positive
rationale: For infants 29 to 60 days, an isolated positive urinalysis does not by itself define high risk for invasive infection when inflammatory markers are normal.

text: A well-appearing 37-day-old infant has fever and abnormal inflammatory markers. What is the best management?
options: Discharge after a negative viral swab
Perform lumbar puncture, start empiric antimicrobials, and hospitalize pending cultures
rationale: Abnormal inflammatory markers place a 29 to 60 day infant in a high-risk group. CSF evaluation, empiric therapy, and hospitalization are recommended.

text: A well-appearing 75-day-old infant has a rectal temperature of 38.1 C and no focal findings. What is the minimum recommended diagnostic testing?
options: No testing if feeding is normal
rationale: For infants 61 to 90 days, testing should include at least urine studies. Broader testing depends on risk and clinical context.

text: Which combination satisfies the updated PECARN low-risk laboratory rule for invasive bacterial infection?
options: Positive urinalysis, ANC 8000 per microlitre, PCT 0.8 ng/mL
Negative urinalysis, ANC 4000 per microlitre or lower, and PCT 0.5 ng/mL or lower
Normal temperature and normal chest radiograph
WBC less than 15000 per microlitre without urine testing
rationale: The updated PECARN rule requires negative urinalysis, ANC no greater than 4000 per microlitre, and procalcitonin no greater than 0.5 ng/mL.

text: Which infant can meet the age component of the Step-by-Step low-risk method?
rationale: The Step-by-Step method applies its low-risk classification to well-appearing infants aged 22 to 90 days and also requires reassuring urine, procalcitonin, CRP, and ANC findings.

text: A 21-day-old infant undergoes lumbar puncture. Which CSF WBC count constitutes pleocytosis under the CPS age-based threshold?
rationale: Pleocytosis is more than 15 WBC/mm3 for infants 28 days or younger. After 28 days, the threshold is more than 9 WBC/mm3.

text: A 50-day-old febrile infant has PCR-confirmed influenza and appears well. Which principle is best?
options: The viral result eliminates the need for urine testing
Lumbar puncture is mandatory in every case
Complete the initial age-based bacterial evaluation, then use the viral result to inform subsequent management
rationale: A confirmed virus lowers but does not eliminate bacterial risk. Initial evaluation remains age-based.

text: Which viral result is specifically less reassuring in a febrile infant 90 days or younger?
rationale: Rhinovirus may reflect prolonged or asymptomatic shedding and is less reassuring than many other detected respiratory viruses.

text: A 3-week-old infant has a rectal temperature of 35.8 C and poor feeding. What is the best principle?
options: Manage the infant using the same infection-focused approach as a febrile young infant
Use an axillary temperature to cancel the rectal result
rationale: A temperature below 36.0 C is associated with infection risk in young infants and should trigger careful evaluation.

text: A 12-day-old febrile infant has vesicular lesions and a seizure. What additional management is most appropriate?
options: No HSV evaluation if the mother reports no herpes history
Obtain CSF for HSV testing and start empiric IV acyclovir
Wait for bacterial cultures before considering HSV
rationale: Very young age, seizures, and vesicular rash are major HSV risk features. At-risk infants need HSV testing and empiric IV acyclovir.

text: A well-appearing 45-day-old infant has a presumed isolated UTI, normal inflammatory markers, and reliable 24-hour follow-up. Which treatment is an acceptable CPS option?
rationale: For a low-risk infant aged 29 to 60 days with suspected UTI, oral cefixime is an accepted option when follow-up is reliable and local susceptibility supports it.

text: A low-risk 70-day-old infant is discharged from the emergency department after evaluation. What follow-up plan is recommended?
options: Follow-up only if fever lasts one week
Healthcare professional follow-up within 24 to 48 hours plus clear return precautions
rationale: Early reassessment and caregiver guidance are essential because young infants can deteriorate despite initially reassuring appearance.

text: A 2-month-old infant develops fever after routine immunization. The fever persists beyond 24 hours. What targeted test is recommended?
rationale: Persistent post-immunization fever carries more bacterial infection risk than fever limited to the first 24 hours. UTI is the key serious bacterial infection to assess.

text: A 12-year-old presents with polyuria, vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, glucose 18 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.2 mmol/L, and venous pH 7.21. Which diagnosis is most likely?
rationale: Paediatric DKA requires hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. This child meets all three criteria.

text: Which laboratory pattern indicates severe paediatric DKA?
options: pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L
rationale: Severe DKA is defined by pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L. Severity is based mainly on acidosis.

text: A 10-year-old with DKA is tachycardic and dehydrated but normotensive. What should be started first?
rationale: Initial management starts with ABC assessment and isotonic fluid. Insulin begins after initial fluid therapy and is never given as a bolus.

text: What is the recommended initial isotonic fluid bolus for most children with DKA?
options: 10 to 20 mL/kg, maximum 1000 mL, over 20 to 30 minutes
No fluid until insulin is running
rationale: Children with DKA should receive 10 to 20 mL/kg of 0.9 percent saline or balanced crystalloid over the first 20 to 30 minutes.

text: A child with DKA has compensated shock. After the initial bolus, perfusion remains poor. What is the best approach?
options: Give additional isotonic fluid in 10 mL/kg increments, up to 40 mL/kg, with paediatric intensivist consultation
rationale: Shock requires faster isotonic fluid resuscitation. Additional 10 mL/kg increments can be used up to 40 mL/kg while obtaining critical care input.

text: When should IV insulin generally be started in paediatric DKA?
options: As a rapid IV bolus on arrival
After the first hour of fluid therapy and only when potassium is above 3.0 mmol/L
Only when glucose is below 10 mmol/L
rationale: Insulin starts after initial fluid expansion and only when potassium is safe. IV insulin bolus is avoided.

text: A child with DKA has potassium 2.8 mmol/L. What is the best next step regarding insulin?
rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells. When potassium is 3.0 mmol/L or lower, replace potassium before starting insulin.

text: A newly diagnosed child with DKA has an initial potassium of 5.4 mmol/L. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Total body potassium is depleted despite the elevated serum value
rationale: Osmotic diuresis causes total body potassium loss. Acidosis and insulin deficiency can make the serum potassium normal or high despite depletion.

text: When should potassium generally be added to IV fluids during paediatric DKA treatment?
options: Before documenting urine output in every case
When measured potassium is below 5 mmol/L and recent urine output is documented
rationale: Potassium commonly falls during therapy. Add potassium when the measured level is below 5 mmol/L after confirming urine output.

text: During treatment, glucose reaches 16 mmol/L while ketoacidosis persists. What is the best next step?
options: Add dextrose to IV fluid and continue insulin to clear ketosis
rationale: Dextrose is added when glucose falls to about 15 to 17 mmol/L so insulin can continue safely until ketosis and acidosis resolve.

text: What is the preferred maximum rate of glucose decline during early paediatric DKA treatment?
options: No more than about 5 mmol/L per hour
Glucose should not fall at all
rationale: Glucose should not fall faster than about 5 mmol/L per hour during early DKA treatment.

text: A child with DKA has measured sodium 132 mmol/L and glucose 25 mmol/L. Using the CPS correction formula, what is the approximate corrected sodium?
rationale: Corrected sodium equals measured sodium plus glucose minus 5, multiplied by 0.3. Here, 132 + 20 x 0.3 = 138 mmol/L.

text: Which statement best describes sodium bicarbonate in routine paediatric DKA?
options: It should be given to every child with pH below 7.3
It should generally be avoided because it increases cerebral injury risk
It is required before the first fluid bolus
rationale: Fluids and insulin correct acidosis. Bicarbonate is generally avoided except for specific indications such as CPR or symptomatic hyperkalemia.

text: Which new finding during DKA treatment is most concerning for cerebral injury?
options: Headache with altered consciousness, hypertension, and bradycardia
rationale: Worsening headache, altered mental status, hypertension, bradycardia, vomiting, respiratory depression, and cranial nerve findings suggest cerebral injury.

text: A child being treated for DKA develops sudden headache, bradycardia, and declining consciousness. What is the best next step?
options: Treat suspected cerebral injury immediately without waiting for cranial imaging
rationale: Cerebral injury is a clinical emergency. Treatment should begin immediately and imaging must not delay osmolar therapy or critical care consultation.

text: Which osmolar therapy is recommended for suspected cerebral injury in paediatric DKA?
options: 3 percent saline 5 mL/kg or mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg
rationale: Either hypertonic saline or mannitol may be used promptly, with critical care consultation and supportive measures.

text: Which IV fluid is acceptable for the initial bolus in paediatric DKA?
options: 0.9 percent saline or a balanced crystalloid such as Ringer’s lactate
rationale: Normal saline and balanced crystalloids are acceptable initial isotonic fluids. Balanced solutions may reduce hyperchloremic acidosis.

text: Which ketone measurement best follows biochemical improvement during DKA?
rationale: Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate tracks changes in pH and bicarbonate better than urine ketones, which can lag or mislead.

text: What is the recommended minimum monitoring frequency during an insulin infusion for paediatric DKA?
options: Glucose every 8 hours and electrolytes daily
No laboratory repetition if symptoms improve
Glucose hourly and laboratory studies at least every 2 hours
rationale: Frequent biochemical and neurologic monitoring is essential. Glucose is checked hourly and broader labs at least every 2 hours during insulin therapy.

text: A child with DKA has abnormal mental status. What is the most appropriate disposition principle?
options: Routine discharge after one fluid bolus
Follow up with primary care in one week
Urgent referral to the nearest tertiary care centre with expert consultation
rationale: Abnormal mental status may indicate cerebral injury and requires urgent escalation. Most children with DKA are admitted and severe cases require critical care input.
